findings.issue_text: [BUG] The login form's zod `formSchema` is never extended with `backupCode` in this diff, so zodResolver strips the field from the values passed to `signIn("credentials", ...)`, and `authorize` never receives it. A user who clicks "Lost access" and enters a valid backup code gets `credentials.backupCode === undefined` in packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts; the `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` guard is false, control falls into the `else if (user.twoFactorEnabled)` branch, `!credentials.totpCode` throws ErrorCode.SecondFactorRequired, and the user is bounced back to the TOTP screen — the entire login-with-backup-code path this PR adds is dead on arrival, and a locked-out user remains locked out. (The `LoginValues` interface at line ~43 declares backupCode and the BackupCode component registers it, but the resolver never forwards it.)

[ADVISORY] Backup-code redemption is a non-atomic read-decrypt-modify-write: the code list is decrypted, `backupCodes[index] = null` is applied in memory, then written back with a separate `prisma.user.update`, with no transaction or unique constraint. Two concurrent sign-in attempts (e.g., double-submit or two tabs) both read the same un-redeemed list, both pass `indexOf`, and both consume the same single-use code — defeating the exactly-once guarantee stated in the new `backup_code_instructions` locale string. A staff-level fix is a transactional update or conditional write keyed on the previous ciphertext.

[ADVISORY] Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the password-visibility toggle button removes it from keyboard tab order in the shared PasswordField used across the entire app. Keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer toggle password visibility on any password field (login, signup, settings, this PR's own EnableTwoFactorModal password step) — a silent accessibility regression in a shared UI component introduced as an incidental formatting change.

[ADVISORY] `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` has no error handling, so corrupt or truncated ciphertext in `user.backupCodes` throws inside the handler and returns a Next.js HTML 500 instead of the JSON `{ error }` shape the contract with DisableTwoFactorModal/login requires. The client's `await response.json()` then throws SyntaxError, and the user sees a generic failure instead of the `incorrect_backup_code`/`missing_backup_codes` messages this PR adds; same unguarded parse is duplicated in next-auth-options.ts where a throw surfaces as an opaque NextAuth error. Rebuttal considered: data is only ever written by setup.ts — but the write goes through `symmetricEncrypt` under an env key that can rotate or be absent per-environment, and there is no version marker on the blob, so the parse failure path is reachable in real deployments.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships a FIXME comment stating the `two-factor-switch` isChecked assertion passes even when the switch is not checked, i.e., the guard protecting the enable-2FA flow is known-broken and knowingly committed. The suite can continue executing the new backup-codes interactions (download/copy/close at lines 110-125) against a state where 2FA was never actually enabled, producing false-positive green runs that mask regressions in the exact feature this PR introduces.

[ADVISORY] The new backup-code validation and redemption logic in `authorize` (and the parallel branch in disable.ts) is non-trivial security-bearing behavior with no test coverage in this diff — the only added test interaction is the e2e UI click-through whose own TODO comments note the file content and clipboard content checks were skipped. A regression in code comparison, dash-stripping, or the re-encrypt-after-redemption write would not be caught by CI; the path most likely to be silently broken (per the zod-stripping defect above) ships with zero executable verification.

[BUG] The missing_backup_codes message promises 'Please generate them in your settings' but the diff adds no settings action to generate backup codes, and for users who cannot log in the settings page is unreachable entirely. Two user groups hit a dead end: (a) users who enabled 2FA before this feature have backupCodes=null (the migration adds a nullable column with no backfill, packages/prisma/migrations/20230804153419_add_backup_codes/migration.sql) and lose their authenticator — the lost_access flow returns 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' while they are locked out of the account; (b) users who consumed all 10 codes get the same message. Generation only exists as a side effect of full TOTP setup (apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts:60-61), which requires either a working authenticator or a successful disable — neither is available to the locked-out user this feature exists to rescue. The feature's core acceptance scenario (recover an account without the authenticator) is unimplemented for these users.

[BUG] Once all backup codes are consumed, login reports 'Backup code is incorrect' (IncorrectBackupCode) instead of MissingBackupCodes, because used codes are stored as JSON nulls and user.backupCodes remains a truthy string. backupCodes[index] = null then JSON.stringify produces '[null,null,...]' (non-empty, truthy), so the `if (!user.backupCodes)` guard at line 136 never fires after exhaustion; indexOf returns -1 and the user at line 144 gets ErrorCode.IncorrectBackupCode — the UI (apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx) then tells them the code is wrong when in fact no valid code exists, sending them into retry loops with a misleading message during exactly the recovery flow this feature targets.

[BUG] Same exhausted-codes defect in the disable endpoint: with all codes used, user.backupCodes is a truthy '[null,...]' string, so line 53's MissingBackupCodes guard is skipped and line 62 returns IncorrectBackupCode. A user trying to disable 2FA via the lost-access path after exhausting their codes sees 'Backup code is incorrect' and retries, when the correct and actionable response is 'No backup codes found' — the DisableTwoFactorModal renders the misleading message at apps/web/components/settings/DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx.

[BUG] Backup code matching is case-sensitive: backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")) rejects uppercase input, and the BackupCode input field sets no autoCapitalize="none"/inputMode to suppress mobile autocapitalize. A user with a valid code who types it with any uppercase character (mobile keyboards autocapitalize the first letter by default; the codes are lowercase hex) gets 'Backup code is incorrect' during account recovery, with no indication the entry is case-sensitive — a valid recovery code is silently rejected.

[BUG] Same case-sensitivity defect in the disable endpoint: indexOf on the user-supplied backup code rejects uppercase input with no normalization. Same failure mode as the login path: valid code typed with uppercase characters returns IncorrectBackupCode from the disable API and the modal shows 'Backup code is incorrect'.

[ADVISORY] No test exercises the two new behavior-bearing paths: login with a backup code (the consumption logic in next-auth-options.ts:130-152) and disabling 2FA with a backup code (disable.ts:47-70); the diff's own TODO comment admits this. A regression in the single-use consumption write (e.g. failing to persist the re-encrypted array, or matching without consuming) would ship unnoticed — the enable-flow test only covers display/download/copy/close, and even those leave '// TODO: check file content' and '// TODO: check clipboard content' unasserted, so the download blob and clipboard payloads are verified by nothing.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a FIXME acknowledging that expect(page.locator(`[data-testid=two-factor-switch]`).isChecked()).toBeTruthy() passes vacuously (isChecked() returns a Promise, and any Promise is truthy) but leaves the broken assertion in place. The 2FA-enable assertion in the shared fixture setup can never fail, so the e2e suite reports enable success even when the toggle was not actually flipped — every downstream assertion in this describe block rests on an unverified precondition, weakening the only coverage this feature has.

[ADVISORY] At the DisplayBackupCodes step, Escape or outside-click closes the dialog via onOpenChange without calling onEnable() or resetState(), unlike the explicit close button which does both. A user who dismisses the dialog at the backup-codes step (the easiest way to lose a one-time secrets view) skips the parent's onEnable callback, so the parent's 2FA state is not refreshed even though 2FA is now enabled server-side, and the modal's internal step state remains DisplayBackupCodes with stale codes instead of resetting to ConfirmPassword — behavior diverges between the close button and the standard dismiss gesture on a screen the user must not skip.

[ADVISORY] The blob object URL created at setBackupCodesUrl is only revoked when a subsequent setup runs (line 98); dialog close, unmount, and completed setup all leak the URL. Each setup attempt in a long-lived SPA session leaks an object URL holding the unencrypted backup codes; combined with the fact that resetState() never clears backupCodes/backupCodesUrl, the plaintext codes remain reachable in page memory (and via the still-live URL) after the user believes the display step is over.

[ADVISORY] The new component in BackupCode.tsx is exported as `function TwoFactor`, a copy-paste of the TwoFactor component that was never renamed. Any future reader grepping for TwoFactor finds two unrelated components (the 6-digit TOTP input and the backup-code input), and imports read `import BackupCode from .../BackupCode` while the symbol is TwoFactor — the next change to either 2FA input risks being applied to the wrong component.

[BUG] The login form's zod schema (formSchema) is not updated anywhere in this diff to include backupCode, so zodResolver's parsed output strips the newly registered backupCode field and the sign-in call submits backupCode: undefined. A user signing in with a backup code hits the server's `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` branch with credentials.backupCode undefined, falls into the TOTP branch, and gets SecondFactorRequired back — the backup-code login path added by this PR can never succeed from the login page.

[ADVISORY] The new missing_backup_codes copy instructs users to 'generate them in your settings', but the diff adds no standalone backup-code regeneration flow — the only generator is the setup endpoint inside the enable-2FA wizard, which is unreachable while 2FA is enabled. Users who enabled 2FA before this feature (backupCodes is null) and who lose their authenticator see a directive to a settings action that does not exist; the only real path is disable-2FA-then-re-enable, which itself requires a working TOTP code — exactly what a 'lost access' user lacks. Codes are also displayed only once with no 'regenerate' affordance, so a user who closes the DisplayBackupCodes step without saving has no recovery in settings either.

[ADVISORY] Backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-modify-write (read decrypted array from the already-fetched user row, indexOf, then prisma.user.update), so the 'used exactly once' invariant promised by the new backup_code_instructions copy is not enforced under concurrency. Two concurrent sign-ins with the same backup code both pass the indexOf check before either update lands, and both proceed to session creation — a single leaked code yields two working sessions instead of one, silently contradicting the single-use guarantee shown to users.

[ADVISORY] The enable-success path now calls setStep(DisplayBackupCodes) instead of onEnable(), and onEnable is only invoked from the explicit 'close' button, so dismissing the dialog by any other route (Escape key, overlay click via onOpenChange) completes 2FA enablement without ever firing onEnable. A user who enables 2FA and then dismisses the backup-codes dialog via Escape leaves the parent settings page state un-updated (still showing 2FA as disabled), and the modal component retains step=DisplayBackupCodes state, so a later reopen shows the backup-codes screen out of sequence instead of the password step.

[ADVISORY] The tabIndex={-1} on the password-visibility toggle is untraceable to the backup-codes requirement and silently changes keyboard behavior of every PasswordField across the app, not just the two modals touched in this PR. Keyboard-only users lose the ability to reach the show/hide-password toggle via Tab in all password fields app-wide (login, signup, password reset, admin invite, etc.) — an accessibility regression introduced by a shared-UI edit buried in a 2FA feature diff, with no requirement in the PR scope accounting for it.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a FIXME stating the two-factor-switch assertion in this test 'passes even when switch is not checked' but ships the broken assertion unchanged, and adds the backup-code download/copy checks only as TODOs (file content and clipboard content are never verified). The suite continues to green-light the enable-2FA flow even when the toggle silently fails to persist, and the new backup-code e2e coverage asserts only that buttons are clickable — a regression that produces empty or wrong download/clipboard content passes CI, which is precisely the failure mode these new assertions were added to catch.

[ADVISORY] The new BackupCode component is internally declared as `export default function TwoFactor(...)`, duplicating the exact component name of the existing TwoFactor component in the sibling file. Anyone debugging a backup-code issue and jumping to definition lands on a component named TwoFactor, and two same-named default exports in the same auth directory make future grep-based refactors (renames, import audits) error-prone — the next contributor must disambiguate by file path alone.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption is an unprotected read-modify-write (decrypt JSON, indexOf, null one entry, re-encrypt, blind UPDATE), so two concurrent logins with the same backup code both succeed, and two concurrent logins with different codes clobber each other's write leaving a consumed code still valid. The single-use invariant advertised in the UI ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') is violable: an attacker with a leaked code (or a user with two tabs) races two login requests and both authorize; conversely a lost update re-validates a code the user believes is burned. There is no SELECT FOR UPDATE, no optimistic-concurrency version, and no conditional UPDATE guarding the read-decrypt-mutate-encrypt-write sequence.

[ADVISORY] Storing the backup codes as a single encrypted JSON array in one nullable TEXT column is the wrong data structure for a single-use credential set: consumption cannot be made atomic (it is the root cause of the race), and consumed codes are represented only by an implicit null-entry-in-JSON encoding. Every future consumer must replicate the decrypt/parse/mutate/re-encrypt protocol and the null-means-consumed convention (currently duplicated in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts); there is no per-code used_at audit, no way to enforce count or uniqueness at the schema level, and no path to per-code atomic invalidation short of a rewrite to a child table with a used flag/unique index.

[BUG] The disable endpoint calls req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "") with no type validation, so a JSON body with a non-string truthy backupCode (e.g. a number or array) throws TypeError inside the handler and returns a 500 instead of the 4xx the error-code contract promises. A crafted or buggy client POST to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable with backupCode: 1 bypasses the MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode 400 responses and produces an unhandled 500; the modal's response.json() then fails against the non-JSON error page, collapsing to the generic something_went_wrong path.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code verification block (env-key guard, decrypt, JSON.parse, dash-stripping indexOf, consume) is hand-duplicated in the login authorize handler and again in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts, with already-divergent consumption semantics (login nulls one entry; disable wipes all codes) and no shared helper. Any future fix — case normalization on comparison, attempt throttling, a code-format change, fixing the race — must be found and applied in two independently maintained copies; the copies have already drifted (one consumes, one deletes wholesale), and the next editor has no signal that the twin exists.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code physical format (5 random bytes -> 10 lowercase hex chars, displayed as XXXXX-XXXXX) is encoded as unprovenanced literals in four places across three files: crypto.randomBytes(5) in setup.ts, formatBackupCode's slice(0,5)/slice(5,10) in EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx, and minLength={10}/maxLength={11} here, with no shared constant. Changing the code length or adding a separator in setup.ts silently breaks the client: the input's minLength/maxLength and the display slicing diverge from generated codes, locking users out of the backup flow with no compile-time or test signal tying the copies together.

[ADVISORY] resetState() clears password, errorMessage, and step but never revokes backupCodesUrl or clears the backupCodes/secret state, so after the modal closes the plaintext backup codes remain in component state and the Blob URL hosting them stays live until the next setup call creates (and revokes) a replacement. The downloadable plaintext-secret blob and the decoded codes outlive the dialog that displayed them, remaining reachable in memory and via the still-valid object URL for the rest of the session — a data-lifecycle gap on a credential the product explicitly tells users to handle once.

[ADVISORY] At the new DisplayBackupCodes step the only in-dialog completion path is the Close button (resetState + onEnable); dismissing the dialog via overlay click, ESC, or the header X calls onOpenChange(false) only, completing 2FA enablement without firing onEnable and without resetting step state. A user who dismisses the dialog at the backup-codes step leaves the parent's two-factor-enabled state unrefreshed (previously every completion path called onEnable), and because component state persists across open/close, reopening the modal resurrects the stale DisplayBackupCodes step with the old codes instead of the ConfirmPassword flow.

[BUG] The enable flow silently changed its completion contract: on successful TOTP verification the code that called onEnable() was replaced with setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes), so the parent's enabled-callback now only fires if the user clicks the specific 'close' button on the backup-codes step. If the user dismisses the dialog via Escape or backdrop click (the Dialog's onOpenChange path) while on the DisplayBackupCodes step, neither onEnable() nor resetState() runs: the server has twoFactorEnabled=true but the parent still renders the settings page as if 2FA is disabled, and the modal component (which stays mounted) reopens stuck on the backup-codes step. This is an objective change from 'TOTP verification completes enablement' to 'viewing backup codes is a mandatory gate' that no human sign-off is recorded for.

[BUG] The login page collects a backupCode field (added to LoginValues and registered by the new BackupCode component) but the diff contains no change to handleSignIn, so the signIn('credentials', ...) call still forwards only the old fields and never sends backupCode to the authorize() handler. The flagship lost-access path is dead on arrival: a user on the backup-code screen submits with an empty/absent backupCode, next-auth-options.ts:131 (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode) is falsy, the TOTP branch runs with no totpCode, and the user is bounced back to SecondFactorRequired / incorrect-2fa errors in a loop. The author's own TODO at apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts:12 confirms no e2e test exercises login with a backup code, so nothing catches this.

[BUG] The setup endpoint now generates and persists fresh backup codes (overwriting user.backupCodes) at the password-confirmation step, before the user has completed setup or ever seen the new codes. A user with working 2FA who re-runs setup and then cancels at the QR-scan or TOTP step has already had every previously issued backup code silently destroyed and replaced by codes they were never shown — their printed/saved recovery codes stop working with no confirmation prompt accepting that destruction. This is a destructive side effect added to a step whose accepted objective was only 'provision a TOTP secret'.

[BUG] Backup-code matching compares the raw user input against lowercase hex codes (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex')) normalizing only the dash (replaceAll('-', '')), not case or whitespace. A user who types a valid code with any uppercase letter (or surrounding space) into the BackupCode field gets ErrorCode.IncorrectBackupCode and is told their valid recovery code is wrong — and on the login path the code is then permanently consumed? No, it is not consumed here, but the user has no way to know case matters; the same unnormalized check is duplicated in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts (~line 60), where a case-mismatch during disable also fails.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code verification block (decrypt, JSON.parse, dash-stripped indexOf) is hand-duplicated verbatim between next-auth-options.ts authorize() and apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts, and the two copies have already drifted in behavior: the login copy consumes the used code and re-encrypts, the disable copy does not (relying on the trailing backupCodes: null). Any future change to the code format or storage (e.g., hashing codes at rest, changing length, case normalization) must be applied in two places plus the client-side constants in BackupCode.tsx (minLength 10/maxLength 11) and setup.ts (5-byte generation); a one-sided update produces a login path that accepts codes the disable path rejects or vice versa. Extracting a shared verify/consume helper deletes an entire class of divergence.

[ADVISORY] The diff codifies a known-broken assertion instead of fixing it: the added FIXME comment states the two-factor-switch isChecked() check 'passes even when switch is not checked', and the weaker assertion is left as the gate for the enable flow in CI. A regression that silently fails to enable 2FA passes this test suite green, which is exactly how an intent drift in the enable flow (e.g., the onEnable() -> setStep() change) ships unnoticed; the objective of the test was weakened without a tracked fix.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships the two new security-critical paths — logging in with a backup code and disabling 2FA with a backup code — with zero test coverage, acknowledged by the author's own 'TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup' comment. Both paths involve destructive, hard-to-reverse state changes (consuming codes, nulling backupCodes); a regression in either (e.g., the missing backupCode forwarding in login.tsx, or the disable branch never matching) would reach users before any test fails, and recovery requires support intervention since the user has lost their second factor.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-decrypt/verify/encrypt-write sequence, so two concurrent sign-ins with the same single-use code both pass `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` against the same pre-write snapshot and both succeed. The single-use invariant the feature promises ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') is broken: a possessor of one backup code can race concurrent sign-in requests to mint multiple sessions from one code, and interleaved writes also resurrect already-burned codes (two requests each write back the other's code as still-valid, since the full list is re-encrypted from a stale snapshot rather than using a conditional/transactional update).

[ADVISORY] The handler calls `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` with no type/format validation, so a JSON body like {"backupCode": 123}, {"backupCode": null}, or {"backupCode": {}} throws `TypeError: req.body.backupCode.replaceAll is not a function`. Any authenticated user posting a non-string backupCode to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable gets an unhandled 500 (HTML error page) instead of the 4xx the ErrorCode contract promises; the same unvalidated value flows into `backupCodes.indexOf` with no length/charset constraint.

[ADVISORY] `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` runs with no try/catch, so malformed stored ciphertext (e.g. after a CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY change or a corrupted row) throws inside the handler. The user is locked out of the disable-via-backup-code path with an unhandled 500 rather than a 400 with a actionable error, and the same throw in the login path (packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts:138) makes the lost-authenticator recovery flow fail opaquely — precisely the scenario this feature exists for.

[ADVISORY] The authorize() backup-code path parses the decrypted backupCodes blob with an unguarded `JSON.parse`, so any decrypt/parse failure throws out of NextAuth's credentials authorize. A user whose stored backupCodes blob cannot be decrypted/parsed (key rotation, legacy row, corrupted value) gets an opaque sign-in failure with no route to recovery, and the thrown error bypasses the structured ErrorCode handling the login page implements for the well-formed failure cases.

[ADVISORY] The new `missing_backup_codes` copy instructs users to 'generate them in your settings', but the diff adds no settings UI or API to view or regenerate backup codes — codes are only emitted once, inside the EnableTwoFactorModal setup flow, and are nulled on disable. Users who hit MissingBackupCodes at login (e.g. they closed the setup dialog without saving) are directed to a flow that does not exist; their only actual path is re-running 2FA setup, which silently rotates their TOTP secret and invalidates their enrolled authenticator — a confusing account-recovery dead end.

[BUG] The diff adds a FIXME comment above `await expect(page.locator(`[data-testid=two-factor-switch]`).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` acknowledging that this assertion passes even when the switch is not checked, but leaves the false-confidence assertion in place unmodified. The enable-2FA e2e test reports a green checkmark for 'two factor is enabled' even when the toggle was never actually enabled, so a regression that silently fails to persist twoFactorEnabled would pass this test and only be caught by the later data-state="checked" assertion (which covers visibility, not the login path).

[ADVISORY] The copy-button test only waits for `toast-success` and contains a TODO admitting clipboard content is never checked, so the test verifies the toast, not the copy behavior. The test passes even if `navigator.clipboard.writeText` fails or writes the wrong content (e.g. codes not dash-formatted or joined incorrectly), because the toast is shown unconditionally after the click regardless of whether the clipboard write succeeded; a future regression in the copied format or a clipboard permission failure ships undetected.

[ADVISORY] The download-button test asserts only `download.suggestedFilename()` equals the literal 'cal-backup-codes.txt' that the component hardcodes in its own `download` attribute, with a TODO admitting file content is never checked. The test mirrors the implementation constant and verifies nothing about the payload: if the Blob is built from the wrong source (e.g. unformatted raw hex codes instead of `formatBackupCode` output, or an empty array when `body.backupCodes` is undefined) the download still produces a file named cal-backup-codes.txt and the test stays green, leaving users with a backup file that doesn't match what the UI displays.

[ADVISORY] The new backup-code login branch — including the single-use consumption logic (`backupCodes[index] = null` then re-encrypt) and the IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes error paths — has no test coverage anywhere in this diff; the only test files changed are apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts (which covers only the enable flow and has a TODO saying 'add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup') and packages/lib/test/builder.ts (fixture default only). Regressions in the highest-stakes new logic — a used backup code not being invalidated (code reuse), the null-slot re-encryption corrupting remaining codes so subsequent valid codes are rejected, or the branch leaking codes when `credentials.backupCode` is set but twoFactorEnabled is false — all pass CI; a user whose backup code is accepted but not consumed retains a permanently valid fallback credential.

[ADVISORY] The new backup-code branch in the disable endpoint (MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode responses and the code path that proceeds to null out all backupCodes) has no test in this diff — apps/web/playwright/login.2fa.e2e.ts only exercises the enable/backup-codes-display flow, and no unit spec for this handler is added or modified. A regression that lets 2FA be disabled without a valid second factor (e.g. the backupCode branch being skipped so the request falls through to the totp branch, or `req.body.backupCode` being an empty string truthy-checking incorrectly) or that fails to delete stored codes on disable would ship uncaught; the e2e test's own TODO acknowledges this gap ('login + disabling 2fa with backup').

[BUG] The setup endpoint unconditionally overwrites user.backupCodes with a freshly generated set on every POST, with no guard for a user who already has 2FA enabled and valid backup codes stored. A user (or anyone with their session, e.g. via direct API call) who triggers /api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup while 2FA is enabled silently destroys the backup codes the user previously saved/downloaded; if the new setup flow is then abandoned before the new codes are displayed (the DisplayBackupCodes step only appears after enable succeeds), the user is left with zero usable backup codes and no way to regenerate without logging in. The data is overwritten in place with no export/backup step — the exact silent-data-loss shape this endpoint's prior code only had for twoFactorSecret.

[BUG] The backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-modify-write (decrypt → indexOf → null the index → re-encrypt whole array) with no transaction or row lock, so concurrent logins race on the same user row. Two parallel login attempts with the same backup code both decrypt the original array, both find the code at the same index, and both succeed — the 'exactly once' guarantee the locale string promises is broken. Conversely, two logins with different codes produce a lost update: the second prisma.user.update overwrites the first, resurrecting the code the first login consumed, so a used code becomes valid again.

[ADVISORY] Existing users who enabled 2FA before this release have backupCodes = NULL in the database with no backfill possible, so the new lost-access flow always dead-ends for them with the MissingBackupCodes error whose message instructs 'Please generate them in your settings'. Every pre-existing 2FA user who loses their authenticator device is shown a recovery path that cannot ever succeed: they cannot log in to reach settings (2FA is required), so the 'Lost access' button presents an unreachable escape hatch instead of an account-recovery channel. The migration adds the column safely (nullable), but the deploy permanently strands the pre-existing population in this dead end until they independently log in and complete a new setup.

[BUG] The backup-code branch performs an unguarded JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...)) and req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""), both of which throw raw exceptions that produce a Next.js 500 HTML response instead of the JSON {error} shape every other failure path in this handler returns. When the stored backupCodes ciphertext is undecryptable (key rotation, corrupted row) or the client sends a non-string backupCode (a number or array is truthy but has no replaceAll, throwing TypeError), the handler crashes with a 500 whose body fails the client's `await response.json()` in DisableTwoFactorModal, degrading a recoverable input/4xx situation into an opaque server error; a legacy user with a stale backupCodes value can never disable 2FA via backup code.

[BUG] The copy button calls navigator.clipboard.writeText without awaiting or catching it and shows the "backup_codes_copied" success toast unconditionally, so clipboard failure is reported as success. When the clipboard write rejects (insecure context, denied permission, non-focused document) the unhandled rejection is silent while the user sees "Backup codes copied!"; in a non-secure context navigator.clipboard is undefined and the onClick throws with no feedback at all. Backup codes are displayed exactly once, so a user who trusts the toast and closes the dialog permanently loses the only copy they were shown.

[BUG] Closing the dialog via Escape, overlay click, or the dialog's built-in close at the DisplayBackupCodes step invokes only onOpenChange, skipping both onEnable() and resetState(), which the Close button path performs. The verification step has already set twoFactorEnabled=true server-side, but the parent is never notified (onEnable not called), so the settings page continues to show 2FA as disabled while it is enabled; additionally the modal's step state stays at DisplayBackupCodes, so reopening the dialog shows the stale backup-codes screen instead of the expected ConfirmPassword entry step.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write (decrypt array, indexOf, overwrite the whole re-encrypted array) with no transaction or row lock, so concurrent sign-ins with the same code both pass verification. Two concurrent sign-ins with the same backup code both pass the indexOf check before either update lands, and both proceed to session creation — a single leaked code yields two working sessions instead of one, silently contradicting the single-use guarantee shown to users.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, backup-code use is implemented as a non-atomic read/modify/write: it decrypts `user.backupCodes`, does `indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))`, then performs `await prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), ...) }})`. There is no transaction or conditional update that ensures the code wasn’t simultaneously consumed by another request. Two concurrent sign-ins can both pass the `indexOf` check on the same decrypted snapshot before either update commits, resulting in two successful logins with one backup code—contradicting the “used exactly once” promise in `backup_code_instructions`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Backup-code consumption is an unprotected read-modify-write (decrypt JSON, indexOf, null one entry, re-encrypt, blind UPDATE), so two concurrent logins with the same backup code both succeed, and two concurrent logins with different codes clobber each other's write leaving a consumed code still valid. The single-use invariant advertised in the UI ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') is violable: an attacker with a leaked code (or a user with two tabs) races two login requests and both authorize; conversely a lost update re-validates a code the user believes is burned. There is no SELECT FOR UPDATE, no optimistic-concurrency version, and no conditional UPDATE guarding the read-decrypt-mutate-encrypt-write sequence.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, backup code verification/consumption is implemented as a read-decrypt-modify-encrypt-write sequence: decrypt `user.backupCodes`, `indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))`, set `backupCodes[index] = null`, then `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), ...) } })`. There is no transaction, row lock, version check, or conditional/atomic update tying the consumed code to the pre-state. Two concurrent logins can both decrypt the same original array and both succeed (same code) or clobber each other (different codes), violating the UI-stated single-use guarantee.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Storing the backup codes as a single encrypted JSON array in one nullable TEXT column is the wrong data structure for a single-use credential set: consumption cannot be made atomic (it is the root cause of the race), and consumed codes are represented only by an implicit null-entry-in-JSON encoding. Every future consumer must replicate the decrypt/parse/mutate/re-encrypt protocol and the null-means-consumed convention (currently duplicated in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts); there is no per-code used_at audit, no way to enforce count or uniqueness at the schema level, and no path to per-code atomic invalidation short of a rewrite to a child table with a used flag/unique index.

adjudication.rationale: The diff stores backup codes as an encrypted JSON array in a single nullable TEXT column (schema.prisma adds `backupCodes String?`; setup.ts writes `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes))`). Consumption is implemented by decrypt/parse, find index, then mutate/re-encrypt (next-auth-options.ts sets `backupCodes[index] = null` and `prisma.user.update(...)`). This is not an atomic “check-and-consume” operation: two concurrent login attempts can both decrypt/see the same unused code, both pass the index check, and both authenticate before either update commits, allowing a nominally single-use backup code to be used more than once. The duplication of this protocol across files (next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts) further shows there is no centralized, schema-enforced mechanism for per-code invalidation/audit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The setup endpoint unconditionally overwrites user.backupCodes with a freshly generated set on every POST, with no guard for a user who already has 2FA enabled and valid backup codes stored. A user (or anyone with their session, e.g. via direct API call) who triggers /api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup while 2FA is enabled silently destroys the backup codes the user previously saved/downloaded; if the new setup flow is then abandoned before the new codes are displayed (the DisplayBackupCodes step only appears after enable succeeds), the user is left with zero usable backup codes and no way to regenerate without logging in. The data is overwritten in place with no export/backup step — the exact silent-data-loss shape this endpoint's prior code only had for twoFactorSecret.

adjudication.rationale: In `/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts`, the handler always generates `backupCodes` and persists them via `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: ..., twoFactorEnabled: false, twoFactorSecret: ... }})` with no guard on existing `user.twoFactorEnabled` or existing `user.backupCodes`. Therefore, if this endpoint is called for a user who already had 2FA enabled and had backup codes stored, the stored backup codes are overwritten (and 2FA is also flipped to `false`) before the UI guarantees the user has exported/seen the new codes (EnableTwoFactorModal only displays them at `DisplayBackupCodes`, after enable succeeds). This is verifiable silent state/data clobbering introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-modify-write (decrypt → indexOf → null the index → re-encrypt whole array) with no transaction or row lock, so concurrent logins race on the same user row. Two parallel login attempts with the same backup code both decrypt the original array, both find the code at the same index, and both succeed — the 'exactly once' guarantee the locale string promises is broken. Conversely, two logins with different codes produce a lost update: the second prisma.user.update overwrites the first, resurrecting the code the first login consumed, so a used code becomes valid again.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts` the new backup-code path in `authorize()` performs a non-atomic read-modify-write on `user.backupCodes`: decrypt JSON array → `indexOf(credentials.backupCode...)` → set `backupCodes[index] = null` → `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(...) } })`. There is no transaction, conditional update, or row lock, so concurrent logins can race. Two parallel requests with the same code can both pass `indexOf` before either update commits (both succeed), and two requests with different codes can overwrite each other’s updated array (lost update), potentially re-validating a previously consumed code. This breaks the “used exactly once” guarantee stated in the locale string.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Existing users who enabled 2FA before this release have backupCodes = NULL in the database with no backfill possible, so the new lost-access flow always dead-ends for them with the MissingBackupCodes error whose message instructs 'Please generate them in your settings'. Every pre-existing 2FA user who loses their authenticator device is shown a recovery path that cannot ever succeed: they cannot log in to reach settings (2FA is required), so the 'Lost access' button presents an unreachable escape hatch instead of an account-recovery channel. The migration adds the column safely (nullable), but the deploy permanently strands the pre-existing population in this dead end until they independently log in and complete a new setup.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new “Lost access” backup-code login path (apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx toggles to <BackupCode/> and next-auth authorize checks credentials.backupCode). However, the only place backupCodes are generated/stored is the new 2FA setup endpoint (apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts stores user.backupCodes). Existing users who already had twoFactorEnabled=true before this change will have backupCodes=NULL (migration adds a nullable column with no backfill), and next-auth explicitly throws MissingBackupCodes when user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode && !user.backupCodes (packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts). The UI maps that to the message “Please generate them in your settings.”, which is unreachable if the user has lost their authenticator and cannot complete TOTP login. Thus the newly added recovery option is a dead-end for that pre-existing 2FA population.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The backup-code branch performs an unguarded JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...)) and req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""), both of which throw raw exceptions that produce a Next.js 500 HTML response instead of the JSON {error} shape every other failure path in this handler returns. When the stored backupCodes ciphertext is undecryptable (key rotation, corrupted row) or the client sends a non-string backupCode (a number or array is truthy but has no replaceAll, throwing TypeError), the handler crashes with a 500 whose body fails the client's `await response.json()` in DisableTwoFactorModal, degrading a recoverable input/4xx situation into an opaque server error; a legacy user with a stale backupCodes value can never disable 2FA via backup code.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the new backup-code path does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` with no try/catch, and then calls `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` without validating `backupCode` is a string. If the encrypted value is undecryptable/invalid JSON (e.g., key mismatch/corruption) or the client sends a truthy non-string (number/array/object), these lines will throw and the handler will return an unhandled Next.js 500 (likely HTML) instead of the `{ error: ErrorCode.* }` JSON shape used elsewhere in the handler. That can also break the client path that does `await response.json()` in `DisableTwoFactorModal`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The copy button calls navigator.clipboard.writeText without awaiting or catching it and shows the "backup_codes_copied" success toast unconditionally, so clipboard failure is reported as success. When the clipboard write rejects (insecure context, denied permission, non-focused document) the unhandled rejection is silent while the user sees "Backup codes copied!"; in a non-secure context navigator.clipboard is undefined and the onClick throws with no feedback at all. Backup codes are displayed exactly once, so a user who trusts the toast and closes the dialog permanently loses the only copy they were shown.

adjudication.rationale: In EnableTwoFactorModal’s DisplayBackupCodes step, the copy button handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` and immediately calls `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")` without `await`/`.then`/`.catch` or checking `navigator.clipboard` exists (diff: `onClick` for `data-testid="backup-codes-copy"`). If clipboard access is denied, rejected, or unavailable (e.g., insecure context where `navigator.clipboard` is undefined), this either silently fails (promise rejection not handled) or throws, while still showing a success toast in the rejection case. That is incorrect user feedback and can cause users to close the modal believing codes were copied when they weren’t.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Closing the dialog via Escape, overlay click, or the dialog's built-in close at the DisplayBackupCodes step invokes only onOpenChange, skipping both onEnable() and resetState(), which the Close button path performs. The verification step has already set twoFactorEnabled=true server-side, but the parent is never notified (onEnable not called), so the settings page continues to show 2FA as disabled while it is enabled; additionally the modal's step state stays at DisplayBackupCodes, so reopening the dialog shows the stale backup-codes screen instead of the expected ConfirmPassword entry step.

adjudication.rationale: In `EnableTwoFactorModal`, a successful enable (`handleEnable`) no longer calls `onEnable()`; it only does `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` (diff shows `if (response.status === 200) { setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes); return; }`). The only place that calls both `resetState()` and `onEnable()` is the explicit “close” button in the `DisplayBackupCodes` step (`backup-codes-close` handler). However, the modal itself is controlled by `<Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>` and there is no logic to run `resetState()` or `onEnable()` when the dialog is closed via Escape/overlay/built-in close (i.e., via `onOpenChange`). Therefore, closing the dialog at the `DisplayBackupCodes` step can skip notifying the parent (`onEnable` not called) and skip resetting local `step`, leaving stale state when reopened—matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write (decrypt array, indexOf, overwrite the whole re-encrypted array) with no transaction or row lock, so concurrent sign-ins with the same code both pass verification. Two concurrent login attempts with the same backup code (double-submit, retry after a slow response, two tabs) both succeed; worse, if request A consumed code c1 and writes [null,c2] while concurrent request B, which read the pre-A array, consumes c2 and writes [c1,null], the already-burned c1 is resurrected as valid, defeating single-use enforcement; the code is also persisted as consumed before the sign-in flow completes, so a later failure in the same sign-in burns a code the user believes is unused.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, backup-code verification and consumption is implemented as a non-atomic read-modify-write: decrypt `user.backupCodes`, `indexOf(credentials.backupCode...)`, then set `backupCodes[index] = null` and `prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(...) } })`. There is no transaction, row lock, or conditional update guarding against concurrent requests using the same pre-decrypted state, so two concurrent sign-ins can both pass the `indexOf` check and both write updates based on stale arrays, potentially “resurrecting” a previously consumed code. This is a real correctness/security defect exposed by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The missing_backup_codes message "No backup codes found. A user whose 2FA was enabled before this feature (twoFactorEnabled=true, backupCodes=null) who loses their authenticator is fully locked out: login requires a TOTP or backup code, and disabling 2FA in settings also requires a code, so the error's remediation instruction cannot be followed by anyone who actually receives it, misdirecting support and leaving the account unrecoverable via the UI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] setup.ts writes symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY) with no presence guard on the key, unlike the two consumption sites added in this same diff (disable.ts and next-auth-options.ts) which explicitly check for a missing CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY.
